{{Otheruses|Yuga Daigongen (disambiguation)}}
'''Yuga Daigongen''' (瑜伽大権現) is a syncretic deity of {{ill|Mountain worship|fa|کوه‌پرستی|ja|山岳信仰|ko|산악신앙|simple|Mountain worship|zh|山岳信仰|qid=Q93697439|lt=mountain worship}} and {{ill|Shugendō|ca|Shugendo|cs|Šugendó|de|Shugendō|es|Shugendō|fr|Shugendō|it|Shugendō|ja|修験道|ko|수험도|pl|Shugendō|pt|Shugendō|ru|Сюгэндо|simple|Shugendō|sk|Šugendó|sr|Šugendo|tr|Shugendō|zh|修驗道|qid=Q1483875|lt=Shugendō}} originating from {{ill|Bizen Province|bn|বাইজেন প্রদেশ|cs|Provincie Bizen|de|Provinz Bizen|es|Provincia de Bizen|fa|ولایت بیزن|fr|Province de Bizen|gl|Provincia de Bizen|id|Provinsi Bizen|it|Bizen (provincia)|ja|備前国|ko|비젠국|lt|Bidzeno žemė|nl|Bizen (provincie)|pt|Província de Bizen|ru|Бидзэн (провинция)|simple|Bizen Province|sk|Bizen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Бизен|tr|Bizen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Бідзен|zh|備前國|zh_min_nan|Bizen-kok|qid=Q1053688|lt=Bizen Province}}'s {{ill|Yuga Mountain|ja|由加山|qid=Q11577570}}. The deity's {{ill|Honji suijaku|fi|Honji suijaku|fr|Honji suijaku|id|Honji suijaku|it|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹|ko|본지수적|pt|Honji suijaku|zh|本地垂迹说|qid=Q3080781|lt=Honji Buddha}} are {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|qid=Q236242|lt=Amida Nyorai}} and {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|qid=Q854773|lt=Yakushi Nyorai Medicine Buddha}}. During the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|qid=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri}} order in the early Meiji period, the deity was renamed "Sōō Daibosatsu" (相応大菩薩) to comply with the new regulations but has since reverted to its original name and is enshrined at {{ill|Yugasan Rendaiji|ja|瑜伽山蓮台寺}}.

== Origin ==
According to legend, {{ill|Gyōki|ar|جيوكي|de|Gyōki|es|Gyōki|fr|Gyōki|ja|行基|ko|교기 (승려)|pl|Gyōki|ru|Гёки|zh|行基|qid=Q1136664|lt=Gyōki}} received a revelation in a dream saying, "This mountain is a peerless sacred land. Establish a temple here, practice the three mysteries of {{ill|yoga in Buddhism|ja|瑜伽|qid=Q24886203}}, and worship me as Yuga Daigongen." Following this revelation, Gyōki founded the temple on the mountain in the fifth year of {{ill|Tenpyō|br|Tenpyō|ca|Era Tenpyō|de|Tempyō|es|Tenpyō|fa|تنپیو|fr|Ère Tenpyō|ia|Tenpyo|id|Tempyō|it|Tenpyō|ja|天平|ko|덴표|no|Tenpyō|pt|Tenpyō|ru|Тэмпё|simple|Tenpyō|sr|Тенпјо|tr|Tenpyō|uk|Темпьо (ненґо)|zh|天平 (日本)|zh_yue|天平 (日本)|qid=Q1199879|lt=Tenpyō}} (733 CE). He enshrined Amida Nyorai and Yakushi Nyorai, marking the beginning of the Yuga Daigongen faith.<ref>Rendaiji Engi (Temple Record).</ref> 

The faith further developed when Yuga Mountain was referred to as "New Kumano Nachisan," aligning with the {{ill|Five Schools of Shugendō|ja|五流修験道}}. According to the records of the Five Streams’ Honzan-based {{ill|Goryū Sontakuin|ja|五流尊瀧院}}, the mountain's temples—Rendaiji (Nachisan), Goryū Sontakuin (Hongū), and Shokōji (Shingū)—were collectively known as the "New Kumano Gongen Three Shrines."

== Overview ==
Yuga Daigongen is known as the "Deity of Disaster Prevention." The deity was deeply revered by successive lords of the {{ill|Okayama Domain|en|Okayama Domain|qid=Q903497|lt=Okayama Domain}}, starting with {{ill|Ikeda Tsugumasa|en|Ikeda_Tsugumasa|qid=Q28131624|lt=Ikeda Tsugumasa}}. It also became one of the most significant pilgrimage destinations in the {{ill|Seto Inland Sea|en|Seto Inland Sea|qid=Q231312|lt=Seto Inland Sea}} region. Alongside {{ill|Konpira Gongen|ja|金毘羅大権現|lt=Konpira Daigongen}}, it was worshiped as one half of the "Dual Pilgrimage," with devotees visiting both shrines once in their lifetime to pray for the fulfillment of their wishes.<ref name="yugasan">[http://www.yugasan.jp/engi.html Yugasan Rendaiji – Historical Record]</ref>

== Shinbutsu Bunri and Haibutsu Kishaku ==
The {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|qid=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri}} order of 1868, followed by the {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|qid=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku}} movement, led to the abolition of Yuga Daigongen as a Shugendō deity. Although {{ill|Yugasan Rendaiji|ja|瑜伽山蓮台寺}} narrowly avoided closure in 1873, it was forcibly separated into the {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|qid=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}-affiliated Rendaiji and the {{ill|Yuga Shrine|ja|由加神社本宮}}.
